lessons.title: Direct object pronouns (unstressed)
body: They answer 'whom?' or 'what?': Vedo Maria → La vedo.
mi · ti · lo/la · ci · vi · li/le
They go right before the conjugated verb.
Lo and la become l' before a vowel: L'aspetto (I wait for her/him).
Li = masculine plural, le = feminine plural.

lessons.title: Indirect object pronouns (unstressed)
body: They answer 'to whom?': Telefono a Luca → Gli telefono.
mi · ti · gli/le · ci · vi · gli
gli = to him, le = to her, gli = to them (formal: loro, after the verb: Telefono loro).
Careful: le is both 'her' (direct, plural: le vedo = I see them, fem.) and 'to her' (indirect, singular: le telefono).

lessons.title: Reflexive pronouns
body: The action refers back to the subject: Mi alzo presto.
mi · ti · si · ci · vi · si
mi, ti, si can elide before a vowel: M'alzo.

lessons.title: Stressed (tonic) pronouns
body: Direct: me · te · lui/lei · noi · voi · loro
Indirect: a me · a te · a lui/a lei · a noi · a voi · a loro
Use them for contrast (Chiamo te, non lui), after 'e' (Vedo te e lui) and after prepositions (con te, per lei).
Stressed pronouns go after the verb; the unstressed ones go before it.
Without contrast or a preposition, use the unstressed pronoun: Ti chiamo ogni giorno.

lessons.title: Direct, indirect or reflexive? How to tell
body: Direct: it answers 'whom / what?' and the verb has no preposition: Vedo Luca → Lo vedo.
Indirect: it answers 'to whom?' and the verb takes 'a': Telefono a Luca → Gli telefono.
Reflexive: the object is the same person as the subject: Mi lavo (I wash myself).
mi, ti, ci, vi look identical in all three jobs: only the sentence tells you which one it is.

direct3.gender.title: Direct pronoun: masculine or feminine?
points: A direct pronoun replaces the person or thing the verb acts on, with no preposition.
Singular: lo = masculine, la = feminine.
First check the gender of the noun, then pick the pronoun.

direct3.number.title: Direct pronoun: singular or plural?
points: The pronoun must match the number of the noun.
Singular: lo / la. Plural: li (masculine) / le (feminine).

direct3.both.title: Direct pronoun: check gender AND number
points: Ask two questions about the noun: masculine or feminine? singular or plural?
The four forms are lo, la, li, le.

direct3.vs_indirect.title: gli / le (to him / to her) are not direct pronouns
points: Verbs like vedere, chiamare, aiutare, invitare take the person directly: no 'a'.
So the pronoun is direct (lo, la, li, le), not gli.
Watch out: chiamare is direct (chiamo Luca → lo chiamo), but telefonare takes 'a' (telefono a Luca → gli telefono).
English prepositions mislead: listen to, wait for, look for, look at are DIRECT in Italian (ascoltare, aspettare, cercare, guardare take no preposition): Lo ascolto, La aspetto.

direct3.elision_plural.title: Only lo and la drop to l'
points: Before a vowel, lo and la shorten to l': L'aspetto, L'ascolto.
Li and le never shorten: Li aspetto, Le aspetto.
Rule of thumb: an apostrophe means one person or thing (singular).

indirect3.gender.title: Indirect pronoun, singular: gli or le?
points: Indirect = 'to whom?'. The verb takes 'a' + person.
gli = to him (masculine), le = to her (feminine).

indirect3.plural.title: Indirect pronoun, plural: gli
points: For 'to them' use gli, for both masculine and feminine groups.
The formal alternative is loro, placed AFTER the verb: Telefono loro.
Le is only 'to her' (one woman).

indirect3.vs_direct.title: Does the verb take 'a'? Then the pronoun is indirect
points: Verbs like telefonare, parlare, rispondere, scrivere, sorridere take 'a' + person.
For these use gli / le, not lo / la / li.
Compare: vedere (no 'a') → lo vedo; parlare (with 'a') → gli parlo.

indirect3.loro_position.title: loro goes after the verb
points: Loro (to them) is the formal alternative to gli.
It is placed after the verb: Telefono loro, never Loro telefono.
Before the verb use gli: Gli telefono.

person12.person.title: me, you, us: which pronoun?
points: For the person speaking and the person spoken to, direct and indirect pronouns look the same.
Check who the object is in the English sentence.

person12.number.title: Singular or plural: ti vs. vi, mi vs. ci
points: You (one person) = ti. You (several people) = vi.
Me = mi. Us = ci.
The English hint says (sg.) or (pl.).

person12.third_form.title: lo, la, li, le, gli are for him / her / them
points: They refer to a third person.
For me, you, us use mi, ti, ci, vi.

person12.reflexive_overuse.title: si refers back to the subject
points: Si is used when the object is the same person as the subject (himself, herself, themselves).
If the object is someone else (me, you, us), use mi / ti / ci / vi.

reflexive.person.title: Reflexive pronoun: it must match the subject
points: Each person has its own reflexive pronoun.
Before a vowel, mi / ti / si can shorten: M'alzo.

reflexive.vs_object.title: Reflexive verbs do not use lo / la
points: With a reflexive verb the pronoun is mi, ti, si, ci, vi.
Lo / la would mean 'him / her / it' as a separate object: Lo lavo = I wash him/it.

tonic.needs_stressed.title: When you need the stressed form (me, te, lui...)
points: Use the stressed pronoun after the verb for contrast (Chiamo te, non lui).
Also when two pronouns are joined by 'e' (Vedo te e lui).
The short form (ti, lo...) cannot carry the contrast.

tonic.needs_unstressed.title: No contrast: use the short pronoun before the verb
points: Without contrast, emphasis, or a preposition, use mi, ti, lo, la... before the verb.
The stressed form would sound emphatic.

tonic.person.title: The stressed pronouns
points: Make sure you pick the right person.

tonic.missing_a.title: Stressed indirect pronoun needs 'a'
points: The stressed form of an indirect pronoun is 'a' + me / te / lui / lei / noi / voi / loro.
Te alone would be a direct object.
examples: Telefono a te, non a lui.

prep.needs_stressed.title: After a preposition: always the stressed form
points: Mi, ti, lo, la are never used after con, per, di, senza, da...
Use me, te, lui, lei, noi, voi, loro instead.

prep.person.title: Pronouns after a preposition
points: Pick the right person for the stressed pronoun.

identify.direct_as_indirect.title: This pronoun is direct object, not indirect object
points: Direct: it answers 'whom / what?' and the verb takes no preposition (Vedo Luca → Lo vedo).
Indirect: it answers 'to whom?' and the verb takes 'a' (Telefono a Luca → Gli telefono).

identify.direct_as_reflexive.title: This pronoun is direct object, not reflexive
points: Direct: it answers 'whom / what?' and the verb takes no preposition (Vedo Luca → Lo vedo).
Reflexive: the object is the same person as the subject (Mi lavo = I wash myself).

identify.indirect_as_direct.title: This pronoun is indirect object, not direct object
points: Indirect: it answers 'to whom?' and the verb takes 'a' (Telefono a Luca → Gli telefono).
Direct: it answers 'whom / what?' and the verb takes no preposition (Vedo Luca → Lo vedo).

identify.indirect_as_reflexive.title: This pronoun is indirect object, not reflexive
points: Indirect: it answers 'to whom?' and the verb takes 'a' (Telefono a Luca → Gli telefono).
Reflexive: the object is the same person as the subject (Mi lavo = I wash myself).

identify.reflexive_as_direct.title: This pronoun is reflexive, not direct object
points: Reflexive: the object is the same person as the subject (Mi lavo = I wash myself).
Direct: it answers 'whom / what?' and the verb takes no preposition (Vedo Luca → Lo vedo).

identify.reflexive_as_indirect.title: This pronoun is reflexive, not indirect object
points: Reflexive: the object is the same person as the subject (Mi lavo = I wash myself).
Indirect: it answers 'to whom?' and the verb takes 'a' (Telefono a Luca → Gli telefono).
